title: The Nawab of Malerkotla
hook: Sher Muhammad Khan protested the execution of the Sahibzade, and Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Moti Ram Mehra, the cook who carried warm milk up the cold tower. Your line was milk in the cold tower. Did you bring someone something warm? Today, the same town, and a voice raised in the governor's court. Day eight hundred twenty-six.

Sirhind, the governor's court. Two small boys stand before Wazir Khan. The sentence is about to be spoken, and the men around the governor can see where it is going. To object now is to take the wrong side of the man in charge, in public, with your name attached. One of the men in that court is a Muslim nobleman, a guest there, with every reason to keep quiet. He speaks instead. Today: the Nawab of Malerkotla.
screen: `TWO BOYS BEFORE THE GOVERNOR.` → `EVERY REASON TO KEEP QUIET.` → `ONE VOICE OBJECTS.`

segments.voice: His name was Sher Muhammad Khan, the Nawab, the ruler, of a small state called Malerkotla. Tradition says he was present at Sirhind when the governor, Wazir Khan, was deciding what to do with Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, the Guru's younger sons. He was not a friend of the Guru. Tradition even says he had fought against the Guru's forces. And still, when the sentence of death was spoken, he protested. The boys were children, he said, and children must not be punished for what their father had done. Sikhs call his protest the haa da naara, the cry of protest against injustice. Here is the hard part. It didn't work. The governor went ahead. The boys were killed. The Nawab could not save them. So why do Sikhs remember him with such honor? Sikh memory doesn't measure speaking up only by whether it wins. He told the truth in a room that didn't want to hear it, at a cost to himself, for children of another faith. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh heard what the Nawab had done, he blessed him and his town. And Sikhs have honored Malerkotla ever since. Set him beside yesterday's cook with his cup of milk. Two people at Sirhind, a Muslim noble in the court and a cook in the kitchen, who could not change the sentence and still did not look away. One carried something warm up the stairs. The other said, out loud, in front of the governor, that children must not be punished.
screen: `SHER MUHAMMAD KHAN OF MALERKOTLA.` · `CHILDREN MUST NOT BE PUNISHED.` · `IT DID NOT SAVE THEM.` · `THE GURU BLESSED HIS TOWN.` · then, large: `HE SPOKE UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak up for the helpless. Let the breath settle. Think of a room you'll be in soon, a meeting, a group chat, a family table, where someone without much power gets talked about or decided about. A new employee. A kid. Someone who isn't there to defend themselves. Find the sentence you could say. Keep it simple, the way the Nawab's was: that isn't fair, or they're just a child, or let's hear their side. Rehearse it once, quietly, on an out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Malerkotla. The small state whose Nawab, Sher Muhammad Khan, protested in the court at Sirhind that children must not be punished, and whose town Sikhs honor for it. Today's word.

Your line: he spoke up. Today, when someone with less power is being treated unfairly in front of you, say the one simple sentence, even if it doesn't win. Day eight hundred twenty-six, and the end of a week.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Nawab of Malerkotla's protest whenever the story of the Sahibzade is told, especially in the December remembrances, and speak of the town of Malerkotla with gratitude.

original.note: Gurmukhi: haa da naara, the cry of protest; Sikhs use it for the Nawab's protest at Sirhind.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ruler who happened to be in the room.
what it means: a Muslim nobleman who protested in open court that children must not be punished, though it changed nothing.
what a scholar hears: Sikhs keep his haa da naara as a measure of speaking up: honored not for winning, but for telling the truth at a cost, across lines of faith.

The Guru's blessing on the Nawab and Malerkotla: 'tradition says'; confirm. The later history (Malerkotla in 1947) left out on purpose under the claims rule.
